Large-scale military operations around Canton will involve serious

In conclusion, let ne congratulate you on your Christmas
card, which
was certainly original as well as attractive. It would
appear from the artist's impression that the ladies have preserved
their occidental characteristics in spite of the oriental custons,
but the red-buttoned mandarin in the upper right-hand corner looks
as though he might have stepped right out of the royal court in old
Peking •
Very truiy yours,
SWill: H
CHOLIS

PERSONAL
Mr. Harold M. Bixby
Pan American Airways Co.
Manila, Philippine Islands
Dear Harold:
December 30, 1937
I was much interested in your personal letter of December 17
connenting upon recent developments in the war in China. You and I are
seeing this great drama from such widely divergent angles and interpret-
ing it from such different sources of inforsatior that it is very inter-
esting to exchange views, not with the idea that either of us can really
claim to know anything but simply to compare notes, which must undoubtedly
give both of us some advantage in shaping our necessarily varying opin-
ions.
I should like to comment seriatum ou some of your points as
follows:
1. The fact that there was unanimity among the Chinese
political and military leaders with regard to the question of coming to
grips with Japan does not, I fear, mean that such unanimity can neces-
sarily continue unbroken during any long protracted struggle.
Chinese
history is not encouraging in this regard and you know yourself how un-
reliable some of these people are in the face of discouragement and op-
portunities to pull out to their own advantage. We do not know, and
have no means of knowing, how much of any break there has been in the
political and military united front of China, but I think you are assum-
ing a good deal when you assume that it is still unbroken. It may not
crumble as fast as some people expect but I do think it will have a ten-
dency that way.
2. You say the war to date has gone pretty much as the
Chinese anticipated. That is undoubtedly true so far as the map of mili-
tary operations shows the course of hostilities, but I doubt if the Chin-
ese ever anticipated the terrific debacle that they suffered at Nanking
and the very heavy loss of life and supplies (munitions, etc.) which they
have experienced.
3. I am entirely in agreement with you that we cannot judge
the Chinese morale or the feelings of the Chinese soldiers by the effect
that similar conditions mould have On Occidentals. You are probably right
in saying that they will take much more without cracking,
are used to adverse conditions. Nevertheless, there must be a limit to
what even the Chinese coolie can endure, and it would seem that during the
monta of December they just about reached the breaking point.
ASPONSI
